notes.text: Cook 4 patties at a time in a 12-inch skillet. For more than 4, keep the first batch warm on a plate under foil, and wash the tongs and your hands after each batch of raw beef.

move.title: Thick burger, safe middle
move.body: A thick burger has a lot of beef between its two browned sides, and the middle is the last part to get hot. Today you'll shape thick patties, sear them in a skillet, and check the middle with a thermometer until it reaches 160°F, the safe temperature for ground beef.

callback.body: Smash burgers are thin, so they cook through in the time it takes to brown them. A thick patty needs the heat a little lower and a few more minutes, or the outside burns before the middle is safe. That's why this burger gets a thermometer check every time.

why.title: A dimple in the middle
why.body: As a patty cooks, its edges tighten and push the middle up into a dome. Pressing a shallow dent in the center before cooking means it puffs up flat instead, so it cooks evenly and sits flat on the bun.

why.title: Not too hot
why.body: A very hot pan browns the outside fast. That's fine for a thin patty, but a thick one would burn on the outside before its middle got hot. Medium-high heat browns the outside while the middle catches up.

why.title: Leave it alone
why.body: A patty sticks to the pan at first, then lets go once a brown crust forms. Moving or pressing it tears the crust and squeezes out the juices. Flip once, when the timer says, and don't press down with the spatula.

why.title: Check from the side
why.body: The tip of the thermometer is where it reads. Pushed in from the top, the tip can go right through a burger into the hot pan. Slide it in from the side instead, so the tip sits in the very middle, the last part to get hot.

wrong.sign: The outside is burnt but the middle reads under 160°F
wrong.fix: Turn the heat down to medium, flip, and keep cooking, checking every minute. Next batch, start a little lower.

wrong.sign: The patty shrank into a thick ball
wrong.fix: Shape the next ones a little wider than the bun and press a deeper dimple in the middle.

wrong.sign: The patty broke when you flipped it
wrong.fix: It wasn't ready. Wait until the bottom is browned and lets go of the pan before you flip.
Patties are never all the same size. Check each one, and keep cooking the ones that aren't at 160°F yet.

quiz.q: Where does the thermometer go in a thick burger?
choices: In from the side, with the tip in the middle
Straight down from the top until it touches the pan
quiz.explain: The middle is the last part to get hot, so the tip goes there. From the side, it can't poke through into the pan.

quiz.q: Why does a thick burger cook on medium-high, not the highest heat?
choices: So the outside doesn't burn before the middle is safe
quiz.explain: A thick patty needs time for heat to reach the middle. Very high heat would burn the outside first.

steps.text: Slice the tomato into rounds. Pull off a lettuce leaf for each burger, rinse them, and pat them dry. Open the buns.
steps.tip: Get everything ready now. Once the burgers start, you'll be busy at the stove.

steps.text: Divide the beef into {n:burger-buns} even pieces. Shape each one into a patty about ¾ inch thick and a little wider than a bun. Press a shallow dent in the middle of each with your thumb. Set them on the plate and sprinkle both sides with {qty:salt} salt and {qty:black-pepper} pepper.
steps.tip: Handle the beef gently. Pat it into shape instead of squeezing.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw beef or its package touched.
steps.tip: Raw beef can carry germs. Wash before you touch the buns or anything else.

steps.text: Heat the skillet over medium heat. Lay the buns in it, cut side down, until golden, then move them to the serving plates.
Turn the heat up to medium-high. Add the oil and spread it around.
steps.look: The oil shimmers, but isn't smoking.

steps.text: Use the tongs to lay the patties in the pan, dent side up, with space between them.
steps.tip: Lay each one down away from you, so any spatter goes the other way.

steps.text: Wash the tongs in hot, soapy water, and wash your hands. Put the raw-beef plate in the sink.
Leave the patties alone while the first side browns. Don't press them.
steps.look: The bottom edges are deep brown, and the sides are turning gray partway up.

steps.text: Slide the spatula under each patty and flip it once. Cook the second side.
Lay a slice of cheese on each patty if you're using it, and cook 1 more minute.
steps.look: The cheese is soft and starting to melt.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the side of each patty so the tip is in the very middle. Each one needs to read at least 160°F. If one doesn't, cook it 1 more minute and check again.
steps.tip: Wipe the thermometer tip between patties.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Move each patty to a bottom bun with the spatula. Add lettuce and tomato, ketchup or mustard if you're using them, and the top bun.
